source_text: Ἀπλήρωτον δὲ τοῦ πί νειν τὴν ὄρεξιν ἔχειν ἐπινοοῦντες, τὸ ἐναντίον πάσχουσιν ἢ προῄρηνται. Τῷ γὰρ συνεχεῖ τῆς τρυφῆς τὰς αἰσθήσεις ἀπομαραίνουσιν. Ὡς γὰρ τὸ ἄγαν λαμπρὸν ἀμαυροῖ τὰς ὄψεις, καὶ ὥσπερ οἱ τοῖς μεγάλοις ψόφοις κατακρουόμενοι τῇ ἀμετρίᾳ τῆς πληγῆς εἰς τὸ μηδὲ ἀκούειν παντελῶς περιάγονται· οὕτω καὶ οὗτοι λελήθασιν ἑαυτοὺς ὑπὸ τῆς ἄγαν φιληδονίας τὴν ἡδονὴν ἀπολέσαντες. Ἄποιος μὲν γὰρ αὐτοῖς καὶ ὑδατώδης ὁ οἶνος, κἂν ἄκρατος ᾖ· χλιαρὰ δὲ τοῦ νεα ροῦ ἡ ἀντίληψις, κἂν τὸ ἀκραιφνέστατον ᾖ, κἂν αὐτὴ χιὼν, κατασβέσαι τὴν ἔνδον ἐν αὐτοῖς ἐκ τῆς ἀμετρίας τοῦ οἴνου καιομένην φλόγα μὴ δυναμένη. Τίνι οὐαί; τίνι θόρυβος; τίνι κρίσεις; τίνι ἀηδίαι καὶ λέσχαι; τίνι συντρίμματα διακενῆς; τίνος πελιδνοὶ οἱ ὀφθαλμοί; Οὐ τῶν ἐγχρονιζόντων ἐν οἴνῳ, καὶ κατασκοπούντων ποῦ πότοι γίνονται; Τὸ οὐαὶ θρηνῶδές ἐστι ἐπίφθεγμα. Θρήνου δὲ ἄξιοι οἱ μεθύοντες, διότι Μέθυσοι βασιλείαν Θεοῦ οὐ κληρονομήσουσι. Θόρυβος δὲ διὰ τὴν ἐκ τοῦ οἴνου ταραχὴν ἐγγινομένην τοῖς λογισμοῖς. Καὶ ἀηδίαι διὰ τὰς πικρὰς ἐκ τῆς τοῦ πίνειν ἡδονῆς ἀνα δόσεις. Τούτων γὰρ δεσμοῦνται μὲν οἱ πόδες, δεσμοῦνται δὲ χεῖρες ἐκ τῶν ἐπιπεμπομένων αὐτοῖς παρὰ τῆς μέθης ῥευμάτων. Καίτοι καὶ πρὸ τού των τῶν παθῶν, παρ' αὐτὸν τὸν καιρὸν τοῦ πίνειν, τὰ τῶν φρενιτικῶν αὐτοῖς συμπίπτει πάθη. Ὅταν γὰρ πλήρεις αἱ μήνιγγες γένωνται τῆς αἰθάλης, ἣν ὁ οἶνος ἐξατμιζόμενος ἀναφέρει, βάλλεται μὲν ὀδύναις ἀφορήτοις ἡ κεφαλή· μένειν δὲ ὀρθὴ ἐπὶ τῶν ὤμων μὴ δυναμένη, ἄλλοτε ἐπ' ἄλλα καταπίπτει, τοῖς σπονδύλοις ἐνολισθαίνουσα. Λέσχην δὲ λέγει τὴν ἄμετρον ἐν τοῖς συμποσίοις καὶ ἐμφιλόνεικον ὁμιλίαν. Καὶ συντρίμματα διακενῆς γίνεται τοῖς οἰνόφλυξιν, οὐ δυναμένοις ὀρθοῦσθαι ὑπὸ τῆς μέθης. Ἀνατρέπονται γὰρ εἰς παντοῖα πτωμάτων σχήματα, ὥστε ἀναγκαῖον αὐτοὺς ἐπὶ τοῦ σώματος συντρίμματα ἔχειν διακενῆς. Ἀλλὰ τίς εἴπῃ ταῦτα τοῖς οἰνοπλήκτοις; Καρηβαροῦσι γὰρ ἐκ τῆς κραιπάλης, νυστάζουσι, χα σμῶνται, ἀχλὺν βλέπουσι, ναυτιῶσι. Διὰ τοῦτο οὐκ ἀκούουσι τῶν διδασκάλων πολλαχόθεν αὐτοῖς ἐμβοώντων· Μὴ μεθύσκεσθε οἴνῳ, ἐν ᾧ ἐστιν ἀσωτία· καὶ πάλιν· Ἀκόλαστον οἶνος, καὶ ὑβριστικὸν μέθη. Ὧν παρακούοντες, αὐτόθεν ἔχουσι τὰς ἐπικαρπίας τῆς μέθης. Οἰδαίνει μὲν γὰρ ὁ ὄγκος, ὀφθαλμοὶ δίυγροι, στόμα ξηρὸν καὶ διακαές. Ὥσπερ γὰρ αἱ χαράδραι, ἕως μὲν ἂν αὐταῖς ἐπιῤῥέωσιν οἱ χείμαῤῥοι, πλήρεις εἶναι δοκοῦσι, παρελθούσης δὲ τῆς πλημμύρας, ξηραὶ καταλιμπάνονται· οὕτω καὶ τοῖς οἰνόφλυξι τὸ στόμα, ἐλλιμνάζοντος μὲν τοῦ οἴ νου, πλῆρές ἐστί πως καὶ δίυγρον, μικρὸν δὲ παραδραμόντος, ξηρὸν καὶ ἄνικμον ἀπελέγχεται. Παρασυ ρόμενον δὲ ἀεὶ καὶ κατακλυζόμενον τῇ ἀμετρίᾳ τοῦ οἴνου, καὶ τὴν ζωτικὴν ἰκμάδα προσαποβάλλει. Ποία· γὰρ κατασκευὴ ἀνθρώπου οὕτως ἰσχυρὰ, ὥστε τοῖς ἐκ τῆς μέθης κακοῖς ἀντισχεῖν; Τίς γὰρ μηχανὴ τὸ ἀεὶ θερμαινόμενον καὶ ἀεὶ διάβροχον τῷ οἴνῳ γινό μενον σῶμα μὴ οὐχὶ ἔκπλυτον καὶ ἐξίτηλον καὶ διεῤῥυηκὸς γενέσθαι; Ἐντεῦθεν οἱ τρόμοι καὶ αἱ ἀσθένειαι· κοπτομένου γὰρ αὐτοῖς τοῦ πνεύματος ὑπὸ τῆς ἀμετρίας τοῦ οἴνου, καὶ τῶν νεύρων λυομένων τῆς συντονίας, ὁ κλόνος τῷ σύμπαντι ὄγκῳ τοῦ σώ ματος ἐπιγίνεται.
thought_title: Drinkers destroy their own senses and bodies
orientation: Basil continues his description of drunkenness, now explaining how constant indulgence deadens the senses and ruins the body.
pass_a_gloss: But devising to have an unfillable appetite for drinking, they suffer the opposite of what they have chosen. For by the continuity of luxury they deaden the senses. For just as the excessively bright dulls the eyes, and just as those struck by great noises are brought around by the excess of the blow to not hearing at all; so also these men have escaped their own notice, having destroyed the pleasure by excessive love of pleasure. For the wine is to them without quality and watery, even if it be unmixed; and the reception of the fresh wine is lukewarm, even if it be the most unmixed, even if it be snow itself, not being able to quench the flame burning within them from the excess of wine. To whom is woe? To whom is tumult? To whom are judgments? To whom are unpleasantnesses and idle talk? To whom are breakings in vain? Whose eyes are livid? Is it not of those who linger over wine, and who spy out where drinking parties happen? The woe is a lamenting exclamation. And the drunkards are worthy of lament, because drunkards will not inherit the kingdom of God. And tumult because of the disturbance from wine arising in their reasonings. And unpleasantnesses because of the bitter belchings from the pleasure of drinking. For of these men the feet are bound, and the hands are bound from the streams sent upon them by drunkenness. And yet even before these sufferings, at the very time of drinking, the sufferings of the frenzied befall them. For when the membranes become full of the soot which the wine sends up as it evaporates, the head is struck with unbearable pains; and not being able to remain upright on the shoulders, it falls now on one side, now on another, slipping upon the vertebrae. And he calls idle talk the immoderate and quarrelsome conversation in drinking parties. And breakings in vain happen to the wine-bibbers, not being able to stand upright because of drunkenness. For they are overturned into all kinds of shapes of falls, so that it is necessary for them to have breakings on the body in vain. But who would say these things to the wine-stricken? For they are heavy-headed from the hangover, they doze, they yawn, they see a mist, they are nauseated. Therefore they do not hear the teachers shouting to them from many places: Do not be drunk with wine, in which is debauchery; and again: Wine is unrestrained, and drunkenness is insolent. Disobeying these things, they have from the very thing the fruits of drunkenness. For the bulk swells, the eyes are watery, the mouth is dry and burning. For just as the ravines, as long as the winter torrents flow into them, seem to be full, but when the flood has passed, they are left dry; so also for the wine-bibbers the mouth, while the wine pools, is somehow full and watery, but when it has run past a little, it is proven dry and without moisture. And being always swept along and flooded by the excess of wine, it also throws away the vital moisture. For what construction of a man is so strong as to withstand the evils from drunkenness? For what device is there that the body always being heated and always becoming soaked with wine should not become washed out and faded and collapsed? From there the tremblings and the weaknesses; for when their breath is cut short by the excess of wine, and the sinews are loosened from their tension, the shaking comes upon the whole bulk of the body.

pass_b_english: But in devising to have an unfillable appetite for drinking, they suffer the opposite of what they intend. For by the constant indulgence they deaden their senses. Just as excessive brightness dulls the eyes, and just as those struck by great noises are brought by the excess of the blow to the point of hearing nothing at all, so these people have escaped their own notice, having lost the pleasure itself through their excessive love of pleasure. For the wine is to them without quality and watery, even if it is unmixed; and the perception of the fresh drink is faint, even if it is the purest, even if it is snow itself, unable to quench the flame burning within them from the excess of wine. Woe to whom? Tumult to whom? Judgments to whom? Unpleasantnesses and idle talk to whom? Bruises for no reason to whom? Whose eyes are livid? Is it not those who linger over wine, and who spy out where drinking parties happen? The woe is a mournful cry. And drunkards are worthy of mourning, because drunkards will not inherit the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians 6:10). Tumult, because of the disturbance that comes upon their reasoning from wine. And unpleasantnesses, because of the bitter after-effects of the pleasure of drinking. For their feet are bound, and their hands are bound, by the rheums sent upon them from drunkenness. And indeed, even before these sufferings, at the very time of drinking, the afflictions of the frenzied fall upon them. For when the membranes become full of the soot that the wine sends up as it evaporates, the head is struck with unbearable pains; and unable to stay upright on the shoulders, it falls now one way, now another, slipping along the vertebrae. By idle talk he means the immoderate and quarrelsome conversation at drinking parties. And bruises for no reason happen to the wine-bibbers, who cannot stand upright because of drunkenness. For they are overturned into every kind of falling posture, so that they necessarily have bruises for no reason upon their body. But who will say these things to the wine-stricken? For they are heavy-headed from the hangover; they doze, they yawn, they see dimly, they are nauseated. Therefore they do not hear the teachers shouting at them from many directions: Do not get drunk with wine, in which is debauchery (Ephesians 5:18); and again: Wine is unrestrained, and drunkenness is insolent (Proverbs 23:21). Ignoring these things, they have from the very source the fruits of drunkenness. For the bulk swells, the eyes are watery, the mouth is dry and burning. For just as ravines, as long as the torrents flow into them, seem to be full, but when the flood has passed they are left dry, so also the mouth of the wine-bibbers, while the wine is pooling, is somehow full and moist, but when it has run off a little, it is exposed as dry and parched. And being constantly swept along and flooded by the excess of wine, it also loses its vital moisture. For what human constitution is so strong as to withstand the evils from drunkenness? For what device can prevent a body that is always heated and always soaked with wine from becoming washed out, faded, and dissolved? From this come the tremblings and the weaknesses; for when their breath is cut short by the excess of wine, and the nerves are loosened from their tension, the shaking comes upon the whole bulk of the body.

problems.quote: Wine is unrestrained, and drunkenness is insolent (Proverbs 20:1)
problems.why: Proverbs 20:1 LXX reads differently; this citation may not match the quoted words.
problems.fix: Wine is unrestrained, and drunkenness is insolent (Proverbs 20:1)
problems.ruling: Proverbs 20:1 LXX reads οἶνος ἄσωτος, not ἀκόλαστον οἶνος; wrong reference.

problems.quote: the enjoyment of the fresh drink is lukewarm
problems.source_quote: χλιαρὰ δὲ τοῦ νεαροῦ ἡ ἀντίληψις
problems.why: 'Lukewarm' suggests tepid temperature; χλιαρὰ here means 'weak, faint, feeble'—the perception/enjoyment itself is dulled, not warm.
problems.fix: the perception of the fresh drink is faint.
problems.ruling: χλιαρά means 'lukewarm/tepid'; context implies dulled perception, but rendering is within normal range.

problems.quote: the bitter emissions from the pleasure of drinking
problems.source_quote: τὰς πικρὰς ἐκ τῆς τοῦ πίνειν ἡδονῆς ἀναδόσεις
problems.why: 'Emissions' suggests physical discharge; ἀναδόσεις here means 'after-effects, consequences, recoil'—the bitter results/repercussions that follow.
problems.fix: the bitter after-effects of the pleasure of drinking.
problems.ruling: ἀναδόσεις means 'recoil/after-effects'; 'emissions' misleads readers toward physical discharge.

problems.why: The Greek quotes 'μέθυσοι' (drunkards), but 1 Cor 6:10 has 'οὔτε μέθυσοι' in a list; Galatians 5:21 has 'μέθυσοι... βασιλείαν θεοῦ κληρονομήσουσιν' as exact match for this phrasing.
problems.fix: drunkards will not inherit the kingdom of God (Galatians 5:21)

problems.quote: the streams sent upon them from drunkenness
problems.source_quote: τῶν ἐπιπεμπομένων αὐτοῖς παρὰ τῆς μέθης ῥευμάτων
problems.why: ῥεύματα here means 'rheums' or 'fluxes' (medical humors/discharge), not 'streams'; it's bodily fluids causing paralysis, not abstract streams.
problems.fix: by the rheums sent upon them from drunkenness
problems.ruling: ῥεύματα in medical context means bodily fluxes/discharges causing binding of limbs, not 'streams' from drunkenness

last_rejected.quote: The woe is a mournful cry. And drunkards are worthy of mourning
last_rejected.source_quote: Τὸ οὐαὶ θρηνῶδές ἐστι ἐπίφθεγμα. Θρήνου δὲ ἄξιοι οἱ μεθύοντες
last_rejected.why: English hides that Basil is interpreting Isaiah's words, not speaking himself.
last_rejected.fix: 'Woe' is a mournful cry. Those who drink are worthy of mourning
last_rejected.ruling: English accurately renders θρηνῶδές ἐστι ἐπίφθεγμα and θρήνου ἄξιοι; no speaker attribution exists in source.

last_rejected.quote: drunkards will not inherit the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians 6:10)
last_rejected.why: The quotation matches 1 Cor 6:10, but Basil presents it as continuing Isaiah's words, not as Paul's.
last_rejected.fix: drunkards will not inherit the kingdom of God (cf. 1 Corinthians 6:10)
last_rejected.ruling: Source gives no attribution; 1 Cor 6:10 is the correct scripture reference for Μέθυσοι βασιλείαν Θεοῦ οὐ κληρονομήσουσι.

last_rejected.quote: the perception of the fresh drink is faint
last_rejected.source_quote: χλιαρὰ δὲ τοῦ νεαροῦ ἡ ἀντίληψις
last_rejected.why: 'Perception' here refers to the drinker's sensation/taste, not abstract perception; 'faint' understates χλιαρά (lukewarm/tepid).
last_rejected.fix: their sense of the fresh drink is dulled
last_rejected.ruling: χλιαρά means lukewarm/tepid; 'faint' is acceptable. ἀντίληψις as 'perception' covers the drinker's sensation adequately.

last_rejected.why: 'Bulk' is ambiguous; ὄγκος here means belly/stomach (swelling with dropsy-like symptoms).
last_rejected.ruling: ὄγκος means bulk/mass; οἰδαίνει means swells. 'Bulk swells' is literal and adequate; 'belly' is interpretation.

last_rejected.quote: they are heavy-headed from the hangover
last_rejected.why: English reverses cause and effect: they are heavy-headed (a symptom), not heavy-headed 'from' the hangover as if hangover were separate.
last_rejected.fix: their heads are heavy with hangover
last_rejected.ruling: κραιπάλη means hangover/intoxication; καρηβαροῦσι ἐκ τῆς κραιπάλης = 'heavy-headed from the hangover' is correct cause-effect.
